name: Prohormones (1-Andro, 4-AD)

card.summary: Steroid precursors once sold as supplements; androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004 and studies found little muscle benefit.
card.note: Androstenedione is a controlled substance in the US since 2005 and banned by sports bodies.

quick.overview:
Prohormones are compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In the 1990s, androstenedione (4-AD, called andro) was sold over the counter as a supplement for raising testosterone and building muscle, and gained fame through baseball players.

Studies found that a single large dose raised testosterone variably and that daily lower doses had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat. The US classed it as an anabolic steroid in 2004.
quick.mechanism: Androstenedione is a precursor in the pathway to testosterone and estrogens. Oral doses may be converted to testosterone in some people, and estradiol also rose in studies.
quick.risks: The FDA banned its sale in 2004, and a 2004 US law added it to controlled-substance schedules, effective 2005. It is banned by the WADA, the Olympics and major sports leagues. Reported effects in women included masculinization and menstrual disturbance.

lead: Prohormones are precursor compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In bodybuilding and physique-building culture the word usually means androstenedione (4-AD, or "andro") and relatives such as 1-androstenedione, sold over the counter in the 1990s and 2000s as testosterone boosters for people who wanted more muscle, a leaner build and a more muscular look.[1]

The appeal was a chain: if a supplement raised testosterone, users expected harder training, more lean mass and a more muscular physique. Androstenedione is an intermediate in the body's own pathway to testosterone and estrogens, and it was marketed on that basis. It was introduced to the North American market with credit given to Patrick Arnold, and gained fame through use by Major League Baseball players in the 1990s, including Mark McGwire.[1]

Published human studies examined whether the chain held. A 2000 JAMA study found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised serum testosterone in young men, with large individual differences and a rise in estradiol, while a 2006 review found that daily doses of 50 to 100 mg did not change strength, muscle size or body fat.[1] Regulators acted anyway: the IOC banned it in 1997, the FDA banned its sale in April 2004, and it became a US controlled substance in 2005.[1] Later designer prohormones remain discussed on T Nation, usually as a historical chapter of supplement culture.[2][3]

chain: Converted in part to testosterone or estrogens
More training capacity and lean mass, in users' expectation
angle.text: Users took prohormones hoping the conversion to testosterone would help them add muscle and lose fat for a bigger, leaner look. Studies of androstenedione measured testosterone and estradiol changes and tested strength and body-composition outcomes directly, and daily doses of 50 to 100 mg produced no change in those outcomes.[1]

paras: A prohormone is a precursor the body can convert into an active hormone. In the supplement context, Wikipedia describes the most common use as muscle growth, with products marketed as ergogenic or anabolic agents.[13] Androstenedione (4-AD or A4) is an endogenous, weak androgen made in the adrenal glands and gonads; it is an intermediate in the pathway from DHEA to testosterone and estrone, with very low affinity for estrogen receptors of its own.[1] Normal serum levels are roughly 40 to 150 ng/dL in men and 30 to 200 ng/dL in women.[1]

Related products sold under the prohormone label included 1-androstenedione and later designer compounds named after other steroid structures. Wikipedia notes that many such designer prohormones were legal in the US until 1-testosterone was reclassified as a Schedule III drug in 2005, and that the majority have not undergone clinical studies.[13]

In the supplement era, androstenedione was bought for muscle gain, strength and a leaner physique. Forum posters on T Nation describe classmates and gym acquaintances using prohormones as teenagers, and remember the 1990s baseball home-run era as the moment the products entered popular awareness.[2][4][5] Their reminiscences also mention later designer prohormones derived from other steroids, sold in the 2000s and since restricted.

Androstenedione was sold over the counter in the US as a dietary supplement, often called "andro," and Sports Illustrated credits Patrick Arnold with introducing it to the North American market.[1] It became widely known through use in Major League Baseball in the 1990s, including by Mark McGwire.[1]

From 1996 to 2001, Barry McCaffrey, then director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, concluded it could not be classified as an anabolic steroid because there was no proof it built muscle.[1] The IOC banned it in 1997, and the FDA banned sales on April 11, 2004, citing health risks associated with steroids.[1]

The Anabolic Steroid Control Act, introduced in the US Senate on March 12, 2004, took effect on January 20, 2005, and placed anabolic steroids and prohormones under the Controlled Substances Act. Androstenedione is a Schedule III substance in the US; androstenediol was also banned under the act.[1][13] Wikipedia notes that illegal steroids such as 1-testosterone continued to be sold under different chemical names, and in one case a product labelled as 1-androsterone was later found to be 1-testosterone.[13]

sections.h: Key people and the designer-prohormone era
paras: Patrick Arnold, a Connecticut organic chemist who studied chemistry at the University of New Haven, is widely called the "Father of Prohormones." Wikipedia reports that in 1996 he helped bring androstenedione to the North American market, though his company sold it as an ingredient rather than as a branded product.[14] In 2001 his company launched 1-androstenediol (1-AD), one of the designer prohormones that followed andro.[14]

After the January 2005 amendment to the Controlled Substances Act banned prohormones, Arnold's company lost about 60 percent of its sales, according to the same account.[14] Arnold was also involved in the BALCO doping case, supplying steroids that were hard to detect; in 2006 he was sentenced to three months in federal prison followed by three months of house arrest.[14]

The 1-androstenedione and 1-androstenediol products referred to in forums as "1-Andro" belong to this second wave: compounds with altered steroid structures sold under new chemical names after andro itself came under scrutiny. Wikipedia notes that the majority of such designer prohormones have not been clinically studied, and that some products labelled with one name were later found to contain another steroid.[13]

Androstenedione is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency and the Olympic Games, and by MLB, the NFL, the NBA, the NCAA, the USOC and the US military.[1] The Anabolic Steroid Control Act was introduced in the Senate on March 12, 2004, and the FDA banned androstenedione sales on April 11, 2004.[1] Wikipedia observes that androstenedione was legally defined as an anabolic steroid even though scant evidence shows it is anabolic, while the 2006 reviewers who found no effect on strength or body fat at 50 to 100 mg daily advised against use.[1]

Androstenedione is a weak androgen produced in the adrenal glands and gonads. It can be converted to testosterone by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, or to estrone by aromatase.[1] In premenopausal women the adrenal glands and ovaries each produce about half of the roughly 3 mg per day, and secretion of androstenedione and DHEA rises in children around age 6 to 8 (adrenarche).[1] Reviews of hormones and hair follicles describe androstenedione and DHEAS as prohormones of testosterone and DHT, the androgens that drive terminal hair growth.[6]

A 2000 JAMA study found that a single 300 mg oral dose raised serum testosterone in young men over eight hours, while a 100 mg dose had no significant effect, and estradiol rose at both doses with wide individual variation.[1] A 2006 review by Brown, Vukovich and King found that daily doses of 50 or 100 mg had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat; a study using 300 mg combined with other supplements also found no strength gain over controls, and the review authors advised against use.[1]
A sports-science review of dietary supplements noted that few products used by athletes are supported by a sound research base and that some may be harmful.[7]

A study of 10 healthy women given 100 mg reported voice deepening, increased body hair, clitoral enlargement, menstrual irregularities and abnormal bleeding, blood clots and metabolic disruption, according to a 2021 review summarized on Wikipedia.[1] For designer prohormones, Wikipedia lists acne, hair loss, raised heart-disease risk, kidney and liver dysfunction, hypertension and impotence among reported side effects, while noting that research on many of them is limited.[13]

An international analysis bought 634 non-hormonal supplements in 13 countries between 2000 and 2001, following earlier reports that some supplements contained undeclared prohormones.[8] Anti-doping authorities cite this contamination risk when warning athletes.

Androstenedione is prohibited by WADA, the Olympics, and major leagues including MLB, the NFL, the NBA and the NCAA, and by the US military.[1] Its association with the McGwire home-run era continues to appear in T Nation discussions of steroids in sport.[9] A 2002 review, "Prohormones and sport," addressed the topic in the steroid biochemistry literature.[10]

Human studies of androstenedione include the 2000 JAMA study of testosterone response in young men and a 2006 review of strength and body composition outcomes, summarized above.[1] A 2004 multi-country analysis tested supplements for undeclared anabolic steroids.[8] No studies of 1-androstenedione were located.

timeline.event: Patrick Arnold helps introduce androstenedione to the North American market.[14]
White House drug-policy director Barry McCaffrey begins a review, concluding by 2001 that andro could not be classed as an anabolic steroid.[1]
A JAMA study measures testosterone response to oral androstenedione in young men.[1]
Arnold's company launches 1-androstenediol (1-AD), a designer prohormone.[14]
The FDA bans sale on April 11; the Anabolic Steroid Control Act is introduced March 12.[1]
The prohormone ban cuts Arnold's company sales by about 60 percent.[14]
The Anabolic Steroid Control Act takes effect on January 20.[1]
Arnold is sentenced to three months in federal prison over his role in the BALCO case.[14]

lore.intro: Prohormones are remembered in bodybuilding communities as the legal pro-steroid supplements of the 1990s and 2000s, and T Nation members still trade stories about them.[2][4]

claims.claim: Andro raises testosterone and builds muscle
claims.believers: Users and sellers in the supplement era said it acted like a mild steroid, and posters recall classmates who used prohormones.[2][5]
claims.experts: A 2006 review found 50 to 100 mg daily had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat; a 300 mg dose raised testosterone variably.[1]

claims.claim: Prohormones are a legal alternative to steroids
claims.believers: Supplement marketing positioned them as legal and mild; some T Nation posters describe using designer prohormones before moving on to injectable compounds.[11]
claims.experts: The FDA banned androstenedione in 2004 and the US classed it as a controlled anabolic steroid; reported effects in women included masculinization.[1]

claims.claim: Over-the-counter prohormone products are often underdosed
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describes brand-name prohormones as underdosed and expensive.[12]
claims.experts: A 2000 to 2001 international analysis examined 634 supplements for undeclared anabolic steroids.[8]

claims.claim: Newer designer prohormones such as 1-AD were a loophole after andro was banned
claims.believers: Posters recall designer prohormones sold in the 2000s as the next step after andro and before injectable compounds.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports 1-testosterone was reclassified as Schedule III in 2005, the 2005 amendment banned prohormones, and most designer prohormones were never clinically studied.[13][14]
